design_detail: Theoretical, mathematical modelling paper with no new data, by mathematicians and computational neuroscientists. It asks whether the geometry of the simple geometric hallucinations that Klüver sorted into four classes of 'form constants' ((i) gratings, lattices, fretworks, filigrees, honeycombs and chequer-boards; (ii) cobwebs; (iii) tunnels, funnels, alleys, cones and vessels; (iv) spirals) can be explained by the map from the retina to the primary visual cortex (V1, striate cortex) and by V1's local and lateral circuits. Method: a continuum Wilson-Cowan-type model of V1 as a sheet of hypercolumns with every orientation preference represented at every point, local connections within a hypercolumn and weak anisotropic lateral connections that join only patches of the same orientation preference along the axis of that preference; a symmetry analysis showing that this connectivity is invariant under a new 'shift-twist' action of the Euclidean group E(2); linear stability analysis by Rayleigh-Schrödinger perturbation theory; the equivariant branching lemma to find the doubly periodic patterns ('planforms') that can emerge when the resting state becomes unstable, on square, rhombic and hexagonal lattices; cubic amplitude equations for their stability; and an inverse ('double') retinocortical map to draw what each pattern would look like in the visual field. Drug action enters only as a change of parameter that destabilizes the resting state (higher excitability or reduced inhibition). The output is compared by eye with published drawings of hallucinations. It extends the model of Ermentrout & Cowan (1979), co-authored by the corresponding author (pp. 299-330).
can_establish: That a V1-like network with this architecture and symmetry, when pushed past an instability, can produce activity patterns whose images in the visual field resemble each of Klüver's four classes of form constants, and which model assumptions (the spread of lateral connections, the strength of local inhibition) decide which patterns appear.
cannot_establish: That psychedelic or other geometric hallucinations are in fact generated this way in the human brain (no human data are analysed, and the comparison with hallucinations is by eye against a few redrawn images); how any drug produces the instability (hallucinogens appear only as an assumed change in excitability or inhibition, and the same mechanism is applied to flickering light and eye pressure); or anything about the complex, figurative visions people also report, several of which the authors say lie beyond the model.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: no participants. Inputs are published anatomical and physiological findings (cat, macaque, owl monkey and tree shrew V1, plus unpublished owl-monkey data cited as a personal communication; human estimates of V1 area and hypercolumn spacing) and published drawings and descriptions of hallucinations (Klüver, 1966; Knauer & Maloney, 1913; Oster, 1970; Siegel, 1977; Tyler, 1978; Patterson, 1992; Clottes & Lewis-Williams, 1998) (pp. 299-305).
sample.selection_effects: The hallucination images used for comparison are a handful of illustrations redrawn by the authors from secondary sources (popular-science articles, a petroglyph, a book on prehistoric shamans' art), chosen without stated criteria; no systematic sample of what people see is used. The premise that all observers report seeing Klüver's form constants or variations (p. 301) and the figure of 30-40 repetitions of a pattern around the visual field (p. 317) are given without sources.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. Hallucinogens are represented only abstractly: raising the coupling parameter, or equivalently the slope of the neurons' response function by a steady input, changes network excitability, which the authors describe as thought to be one of the possible effects of hallucinogens; an indirect reduction of inhibition is offered as another possibility (p. 311); the Discussion presumes the instability occurs shortly after hallucinogens act on brain-stem nuclei that control cortical excitability (p. 323). No receptor, drug or dose is modelled.

comparison.controls: No empirical comparison. The model is set against the earlier Ermentrout-Cowan model, which had no orientation preference and so could not produce lattice tunnels, honeycombs, certain chequer-boards or cobwebs (p. 303), and, visually, against drawings of hallucinations (p. 317).

outcomes.instruments: Mathematical analysis: eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the linearized model (pp. 309-312), planforms identified from the axial subgroups of the lattice symmetry groups (pp. 312-314), cubic amplitude equations for their selection and stability (pp. 318-323), and visual-field images obtained with single and double inverse retinocortical maps (pp. 314-320).
outcomes.validity_norms: No quantitative test against perceptual or physiological data. Resemblance to form constants is judged by eye (p. 317). Anatomical parameters come largely from other species and are scaled to human V1 with a hypercolumn spacing of about 1.33-2 mm taken from anatomical and psychophysical evidence (p. 304).
outcomes.operationalization: A geometric hallucination is identified with a spatially periodic pattern of V1 activity that branches off the uniform resting state when it becomes unstable. 'Contoured' patterns are lattices of locally oriented edges; 'non-contoured' patterns are contrasting regions of light and dark (pp. 312-314).

analysis.effect_sizes: Not applicable (no statistical estimates). Quantities used or derived: retinocortical map constants w0 = 0.087 and epsilon = 0.051 estimated from published data (Drasdo, 1977) (p. 302); human V1 about 3500 mm2 per hemisphere, a hypercolumn about 2.67 mm2, so about 1300 hypercolumns (p. 305); with a unit length of about 400 micrometres the critical pattern wavelength is given as about 2.66 mm (p. 311); commonly reported hallucinations show 30-40 repetitions around the visual field, corresponding to 2.4-3.2 mm in V1 (p. 317); contour-completing (even) patterns require lateral connections spreading more than 45 degrees (theta0 > pi/4) from the axis of orientation preference (pp. 311, 324).
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable. The authors defer a fuller stability analysis, including higher-order terms, to a separate paper (Bressloff et al., 2000b) (p. 319).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Mathematically, when the resting state of a V1-like sheet with local and weak anisotropic lateral connections loses stability, a finite set of doubly periodic patterns can arise; mapped back to the visual field, non-contoured patterns look like tunnels, funnels and spirals and contoured ones like honeycombs, chequer-boards, lattices and cobwebs. With the strict anisotropy suggested by anatomy, the contoured patterns that appear do not form continuous contours; contour-completing patterns needed lateral connections spreading more than 45 degrees. Square patterns were unstable; rolls, hexagons and triangles could be stable. The resemblance to hallucinations is shown by comparing figures by eye.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion state that the planforms generate representatives of all the form constants and that all the Klüver form constants can now be obtained (pp. 299, 324), qualified in the abstract as resting on the authors' interpretation of the correspondence between V1 patterns and percepts and on the presumed action of hallucinogens. The Discussion concludes that V1 circuits normally involved in detecting oriented edges and processing contours 'are also responsible for the generation of the hallucinatory form constants' (p. 324), which goes beyond a model not tested against physiological or perceptual data, although the abstract frames the same point as an interesting possibility if the mechanism is sited mainly in V1 (p. 300). The authors list limits: continuity of the images across the midline and their stability in the visual field are deferred (p. 301); the restriction to doubly periodic solutions has no formal justification (p. 312); some reported images (a tunnel with reversed magnification, a lattice-tunnel, a complex image after LSD) cannot be understood with the simple model (pp. 325-326).

timeline.event: Klüver's classification of geometric hallucinations into four form constants, cited by this paper from Klüver (1966).

Ermentrout & Cowan: model in which hallucinogens destabilize a two-dimensional sheet of excitatory and inhibitory neurons so that stripes, hexagons or squares of activity form, which the retinocortical map turns into funnels, spirals and chequer-boards; without orientation it cannot produce lattices, honeycombs or cobwebs (as described, p. 303).
Wiener (1994, thesis) and Cowan (1997): preliminary accounts of the extension to orientation-selective cells (as described, p. 304).
Zweck & Williams (2001): basis functions with the same shift-twist symmetry, introduced for an algorithm of contour completion (as described, p. 325).

replication.where_it_stands: A theoretical account. Among the sources read for this card, no empirical test of its predictions (for example the double retinocortical map's predicted orientation changes near the horizontal meridian, detectable with optical imaging, p. 324) has been read. The card supports statements about what the model proposes, what it rests on and what it predicts, not about what happens in the brain during psychedelic use.

The corresponding author, J.D. Cowan, co-authored the earlier model this paper extends (Ermentrout & Cowan, 1979). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the work.

what_would_settle_it: Imaging of V1 activity at sufficient resolution during simple geometric hallucinations induced by a psychedelic or by flickering light, testing for the predicted stripe or lattice patterns with wavelengths of about 2.4-3.2 mm and for the predicted orientation structure, combined with systematic, quantitative reports from observers of which form constants they see and when.

domains.domain: Model assumptions and their empirical support
domains.note: The architecture rests on orientation maps and lateral-connection patterns from cat, macaque, owl monkey and tree shrew (partly unpublished data), scaled to human V1 by a hypercolumn spacing inferred from anatomical and psychophysical evidence; it assumes all orientations at every point, weak lateral connections, a continuum despite pattern wavelengths of about twice the hypercolumn spacing (p. 305), and doubly periodic solutions without formal justification (p. 312), each stated by the authors.

domains.domain: Comparison with the phenomenon it explains
domains.note: The only check against hallucinations is by eye, with a few drawings redrawn from secondary sources (pp. 300-302, 317, 325); there is no quantitative measure of fit and no systematic data on what people see; the repetition figure that sets the expected wavelength is uncited (p. 317).

Hallucinogens enter only as an assumed rise in excitability or fall in inhibition (p. 311); no receptor or pharmacology is modelled, and the same mechanism is applied to flickering light, eye pressure, anaesthetics and the edges of sleep, so nothing in the model is specific to psychedelics.

domains.domain: Sensitivity of the conclusions to parameter choices
domains.note: The abstract says the results are sensitive to the detailed specification of the lateral connectivity (p. 300); the contour-completing patterns that match seen form constants appear only when lateral connections spread more than 45 degrees from the axis of orientation preference, a departure from the strict anisotropy that motivated the model (pp. 311, 324).
Equations, parameter values for the plotted curves and derivations (Appendix A) are printed.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own work
domains.note: Builds on the corresponding author's earlier model (Ermentrout & Cowan, 1979), a thesis and a preliminary account by authors (Wiener, 1994; Cowan, 1997) and the authors' own 2000 papers, with a fuller stability analysis deferred to one of them (p. 319).

Assumptions and interpretations are mostly flagged ('presumed action of hallucinogens', 'given our interpretation', 'intriguing possible scenarios'), but some premises are asserted (all observers see form constants, p. 301), and the Discussion's conclusion that V1 edge circuits are responsible for the form constants is firmer than the abstract's 'interesting possibility' (pp. 300, 324).

domains.domain: Balance (alternative explanations of the form constants)
domains.note: Alternatives are mentioned (filling in by higher areas, V2 for stabilization, dorsal MSTd for some tunnel images, an argument from continuity across the midline for higher levels) but no competing model is developed or compared; a retinal origin is set aside with a brief argument (images seen by blind subjects and in dark rooms, and moving with the eyes) (pp. 300-301, 312, 325-326).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument exists for a theoretical model (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is applied with domains suited to modelling, as on other modelling cards. As mathematics the paper is careful and transparent, and it states its main assumptions. As evidence about psychedelic visuals it is weak: the drug appears only as an abstract parameter shared with flicker and eye pressure, the anatomy comes mainly from other species, and the fit to hallucinations is a visual resemblance to a few redrawn images. The card may be cited for what the model proposes and rests on: that the simple geometric patterns seen on psychedelics and in other conditions fall into Klüver's four classes, that the retina-to-cortex map turns tunnels, funnels and spirals into simple stripes of activity in V1, and that a V1-like network pushed past an instability can generate patterns resembling all four classes; and for its stated predictions. It should not be cited as showing that psychedelic visuals are produced this way, or as an account of how psychedelics act on the brain.

key_findings.finding: The paper takes Klüver's four classes of form constants as the phenomenon to explain ((i) gratings, lattices, fretworks, filigrees, honeycombs and chequer-boards; (ii) cobwebs; (iii) tunnels, funnels, alleys, cones and vessels; (iv) spirals) and investigates mathematically the assumption that the retina-to-V1 map and V1's local and lateral circuits determine their geometry.

Geometric hallucinations are described as occurring after flickering light, certain anaesthetics, on waking or falling asleep, after deep pressure on the eyeballs and shortly after drugs such as LSD and marijuana; they are also seen by blind people and in sealed dark rooms, and they move with the eyes while keeping their positions relative to each other, which the authors take to mean they arise in the brain rather than the eyes; in the authors' view they are generated in V1 and stabilized by V2 and other areas.
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction › (a) Form constants and visual imagery (p. 300, both columns; p. 301, left column, first paragraph)

key_findings.finding: Away from the fovea the retina-to-V1 map behaves like a complex logarithm (constants w0 = 0.087 and epsilon = 0.051 estimated from Drasdo, 1977), so circles in the visual field become vertical lines in V1, rays become horizontal lines and logarithmic spirals become oblique lines: tunnel, funnel and spiral form constants correspond to stripes of neural activity at various angles in V1.
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction › (b) The human retinocortical map (p. 302); (c) Form constants as spontaneous cortical patterns, 1st paragraph (p. 303); Figures 5-7

key_findings.finding: The earlier Ermentrout-Cowan model, in which a Turing-like instability makes stripes, hexagons or squares of activity form in a sheet of excitatory and inhibitory neurons, treats V1 as a 'cortical retina' without orientation preference and so cannot produce lattice tunnels, honeycombs, certain chequer-boards or cobwebs, which look more like lattices of oriented edges.
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction › (c), 2nd paragraph; (d) Orientation tuning in V1, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Anatomical basis of the new model: orientation preference repeats about every 300 micrometres in cat V1 and about every 0.5 mm in macaque V1; nearby cells connect roughly isotropically, while long horizontal axons in layers II-III link patches of similar orientation about every 0.5 mm, running along the axis of their orientation preference (owl monkey, tree shrew); these come almost entirely from excitatory cells, 20% ending on inhibitory cells; human V1 is estimated at about 3500 mm2 per hemisphere with a hypercolumn spacing of about 1.33-2 mm, about 1300 hypercolumns.
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction › (d) Orientation tuning in V1, from the 2nd paragraph to the end of the subsection (pp. 303-304); Figures 8-10; 2(a) The model, left column (p. 305)

key_findings.finding: The drug enters only through the bifurcation parameter: raising global coupling, or equivalently the slope of the neurons' output function through a steady input, changes network excitability, which the authors describe as thought to be one of the possible effects of hallucinogens; hallucinogens might also act indirectly on the balance of inhibition, which could influence which patterns emerge.
key_findings.locator: 3. Linear stability analysis › (c) Marginal stability › (i) Choosing the bifurcation parameter

key_findings.finding: Two families of patterns: if inhibition between neighbouring orientation patches is weak, V1 behaves without intrinsic orientation tuning and non-contoured patterns (light and dark regions) arise, corresponding to tunnels, funnels and spirals; if it is strong, contoured patterns (lattices of oriented edges) arise, corresponding to honeycombs, chequer-boards and cobwebs.
key_findings.locator: 3(d) The Ermentrout-Cowan model revisited (p. 312); 7. Discussion, item (i) of the second list, after the 3rd paragraph (p. 324)

key_findings.finding: With lateral connections strictly along the axis of orientation preference (and acting as inhibitory), the 'odd' contoured patterns are selected, and these do not form continuous contours; the contour-completing 'even' patterns, which recover the form constants missing from the earlier model, appear when lateral connections spread more than 45 degrees (theta0 > pi/4) from that axis.
key_findings.locator: 3(c), right-column paragraph beginning 'An interesting question' and Figure 17 (p. 311); 5(b) Planforms in the visual field, last paragraph (p. 317); 7. Discussion, item (ii) of the second list (p. 324)

key_findings.finding: Stability: on square or rhombic lattices rolls are stable and squares unstable (for contoured patterns on a rhombic lattice, rhombic patterns are stable when the lattice angle lies between 30 and 60 degrees); on hexagonal lattices stable hexagons appear first for even patterns, and hexagons or triangles for odd patterns; the authors note that hallucinations resembling square patterns exist and may be transitional forms.
key_findings.locator: 6. The selection and stability of patterns › (b) (p. 321); (c) and (d) (pp. 322-323); 7. Discussion, item (i) of the second list (p. 324)

key_findings.finding: Scale: commonly reported hallucinations have 30-40 repetitions of the pattern around the visual field, corresponding to 2.4-3.2 mm in V1, the range expected for the model's critical wavelength; with a unit length of about 400 micrometres the paper gives a critical wavelength of about 2.66 mm.
key_findings.locator: 3(c), last paragraph of the left column (p. 311); 5(b) Planforms in the visual field, right column, text after equation (45) (p. 317)
key_findings.note: The 30-40 repetitions figure is not referenced. On the 2.66 mm figure see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: The match with hallucinations is shown by inviting the reader to compare figures: for example the pressure phosphene of Figure 1 with the model pattern of Figure 35a, and the cobweb petroglyph of Figure 4 with Figure 31a.
key_findings.locator: 5(b) Planforms in the visual field, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: Predictions offered for testing: if V1 implements the double retinocortical map, cells tuned to the same relative angle should be preferentially connected, and orientation changes should be relatively large and detectable with optical imaging near the horizontal meridian; reports of a bright white light at the centre of the visual field that expands into a hallucination in about 3 s after LSD and similar drugs would correspond to activity spreading across V1 at about 2.4 cm per second.
key_findings.locator: 7. Discussion, item (ii) of the first list, after the 2nd paragraph (p. 324); item (ii) of the second list (p. 324, continuing on p. 325)

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: continuity of the images across the midline and their stability in the visual field are deferred; the restriction to doubly periodic solutions has no formal justification; some reported images (a tunnel with reversed magnification, a marijuana lattice-tunnel, a complex image after LSD) cannot be understood in terms of the simple model and may involve circuits beyond V1 such as dorsal MSTd, mismatches with a disordered cortical lattice or more than one length scale.
key_findings.locator: 1(a), last paragraph (p. 301); 4. Doubly periodic planforms, 1st paragraph (p. 312); 7. Discussion, item (iv) of the second list (pp. 325-326)

reporting_issues.issue: The wavelength is given as 2 pi (0.400)/qc mm, 'ca. 2.66 mm at the critical wavenumber qc = 1'; at qc = 1 the expression gives 2.51 mm (editors' calculation). 2.66 mm corresponds to qc of about 0.94, close to the critical wavenumber marked in Figure 16a.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; either value lies inside the 2.4-3.2 mm range the authors expect.

reporting_issues.issue: The model V1 domain is described as two pieces of 72 mm along x and 48 mm along y, and the cylindrical period in y is 96 mm (two hemifields of 48 mm), but the same paragraph says the y coordinate changes from -pi/2 to pi/2 'in 72 mm'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; 48 mm fits the 96 mm period used in equation (43).

reporting_issues.issue: Two empirical premises carry no source: that all observers report seeing Klüver's form constants or variations (p. 301), and that commonly reported hallucination patterns have 30-40 repetitions around the visual field (p. 317), which fixes the expected cortical wavelength of 2.4-3.2 mm.
reporting_issues.consequence: The match in scale between model and hallucinations rests on an unreferenced figure.

reporting_issues.issue: The hallucination images against which the model's patterns are compared are redrawn by the authors from secondary sources (Oster, 1970; Siegel, 1977, both in Scientific American; a petroglyph; cave-art illustrations; Tyler, 1978), and one is a petroglyph whose hallucinatory origin is stated as possible ('patterns that may be hallucinatory'), not established.
reporting_issues.consequence: The visual comparison tests resemblance to selected illustrations, not to what people actually report seeing.
